book.title: How to Know a Person
book.subtitle: The Art of Seeing Others Deeply and Being Deeply Seen
book.author_credibility: David Brooks is a long-time New York Times opinion columnist and author of several books on character and social life (The Social Animal, The Road to Character, The Second Mountain). He is not a psychologist or researcher; the book is a synthesis of psychology, philosophy, literature and personal experience. He is candid that he wrote it partly to fix his own reserved, emotionally distant habits, which makes it personal and motivational but also means some advice reflects his temperament and moral outlook more than tested method.
book.evidence_base: Mixed. Some chapters lean on solid peer-reviewed work (Nicholas Epley's lab on deep conversation and perspective getting, Dan McAdams on narrative identity, Big Five personality research, developmental psychology from Erik Erikson and others). Much of the practical advice (Illuminators versus Diminishers, accompaniment, conversation tips, looping, hard conversations) is drawn from essays, philosophers such as Simone Weil, practitioners, interviews and Brooks's own experience. The chapter on supporting a friend in despair rests largely on one case: his friend Peter Marks, who died by suicide after years of depression. Reviewers note the book is engaging but in places anecdotal and thin on step-by-step method.

insights.name: Illuminators versus Diminishers
insights.explanation: Brooks sorts people by the effect they have on others. Diminishers leave you feeling unseen: they steer talk back to themselves, label you quickly, treat you as a means to an end, or simply overlook what you are trying to say. Illuminators leave you feeling bigger and more understood: they are curious, ask follow-up questions, and try to see the world a little from your side. His central claim is that illuminating is a learnable set of skills rather than a personality trait, and that most of us drift into diminishing out of habit, distraction or self-focus rather than malice.
insights.when_to_use: As a quick self-check before and after any conversation that matters: a one-on-one with a report, a first date, dinner with a parent, a networking coffee. Ask afterward: did the other person leave feeling more seen or less seen?
insights.worked_example: After a team lunch, a manager realizes she spent most of it describing her own weekend and answering emails under the table, while a new analyst tried twice to mention a project idea. At the next lunch she sets her phone face down, asks the analyst what drew her to the role, and follows up on the project idea with two specific questions. Same lunch, same people; the difference is whether she was diminishing or illuminating.
common_mistakes: Using the labels to judge others rather than to audit your own behavior.
Assuming warmth alone makes you an illuminator; Brooks stresses that good intentions without listening and questioning skills still leave people unseen.
Performing interest (nodding while waiting to talk) instead of actually being curious.

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 1, 'I See You', early chapters on the power of being seen; also NYT column 'The Essential Skills for Being Human' (Oct 19, 2023).
source.underlying_research: None specific; a conceptual framing. Brooks cites survey data that a majority of Americans report no one knows them well (reported by reviewers as 54 percent), but the Illuminator/Diminisher typology itself is his own.

insights.confidence_rationale: Memorable and practically useful as a reflective lens, but it is an essayist's typology, not a validated construct. The term echoes Liz Wiseman's earlier 'Multipliers versus Diminishers' leadership framing, which is also practitioner-based. Rated Low on evidence, not on usefulness.

insights.name: Accompaniment: walk beside, do not steer
insights.explanation: Before deep knowing comes ordinary companionship: spending unhurried time alongside someone without an agenda to fix, impress or extract. Brooks describes accompaniment as having several qualities: patience (respecting the other person's timetable rather than forcing depth, which he links to Simone Weil's idea of holding back, or 'negative effort'), playfulness (light shared activity where the content matters less than the togetherness), other-centeredness (turning down your own self-importance), and presence (staying with someone rather than rushing to solve). Trust and openness grow out of this shared ordinary time.
insights.when_to_use: Early in any relationship, when someone is going through a hard stretch but is not ready to talk, with teenagers or reserved colleagues, and when rebuilding distance in a family relationship.
insights.worked_example: A father wants to know what is going on with his quiet 15-year-old. Instead of a sit-down talk, he starts driving her to practice and stopping for food afterward, keeping it light. Weeks later, on one of those drives, she brings up a friendship falling apart. At work, a team lead does something similar with a guarded new hire: regular coffee walks with no agenda, which later make a frank conversation about workload possible.
common_mistakes: Treating time together as a setup for the 'real' talk and pushing for disclosure too soon.
Confusing presence with passivity; accompaniment still involves attention and small gestures.
Filling every silence instead of letting the other person set the pace.
situations: Building trust with a guarded new hire
Supporting a friend who will not talk yet

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 1, Chapter 4 'Accompaniment'.
source.underlying_research: Philosophical rather than empirical: Simone Weil (attention, negative effort). No specific study identified in sources reviewed.

insights.confidence_rationale: Chapter existence and its themes (patience, playfulness, presence, other-centeredness) are confirmed by several summaries and a reading guide, but support is philosophical and anecdotal. Plausible and consistent with common relationship wisdom; not tested as stated.

insights.name: Attention is a switch, not a dimmer (be a loud listener)
insights.explanation: Brooks argues that half-attention is visible and diminishing, so attention should be all on or deliberately off. When you listen, make it obvious: an active, responsive body and face, small verbal signals, and follow-up questions that show you tracked what was said. He calls this being a loud listener, and summaries report he endorses the classroom acronym SLANT (sit up, lean forward, ask questions, nod, track the speaker). He also advises hearing the whole point before composing your reply.
insights.when_to_use: Any conversation where the other person is telling you something that matters to them: a report raising a concern, a partner describing a bad day, a client explaining a problem, a video call where cues are weaker.
insights.worked_example: On a video call, an engineer explains why a deadline slipped. Her manager closes his other tabs, keeps his camera on, nods visibly, says 'okay, so the vendor API changed' at a natural pause, and asks what she would need to recover. At home that evening, when his partner starts describing a conflict with her sister, he puts his phone in another room before answering rather than half-listening from the couch.
common_mistakes: Multitasking while saying 'go on, I'm listening'.
Over-performing (constant nodding, exaggerated reactions) so it feels like technique rather than interest.
Planning your response while they are still talking.
steps: Decide: can I give full attention right now? If not, say so and set a time.
Remove the obvious competitors: phone, other tabs, notifications.
Show tracking physically: face them, lean in slightly, keep eye contact natural.
Give small verbal signals and brief recaps at natural pauses.
Wait until they finish the point before forming your reply; then ask one follow-up question about what they said.
situations: Report raising a concern in a one-on-one

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Chapter 6 'Good Talks' (attention as on/off switch, reported around p. 74 by a discussion guide); loud-listener advice reported by several reviewers.
source.underlying_research: No specific study named in sources reviewed. SLANT is a classroom engagement routine associated with charter-school practice (often credited to Doug Lemov's Teach Like a Champion); attribution within the book not verified.

insights.confidence_rationale: Brooks's support is experiential, but the general point that visibly attentive, responsive listening makes speakers feel understood is consistent with broader listening research not cited here. Specific tactics (SLANT) are practitioner tools rather than tested conversational interventions.

insights.name: Deep talk is less awkward than you fear
insights.explanation: People systematically expect deeper conversations with strangers or acquaintances to be more awkward and less enjoyable than they turn out to be, largely because they underestimate how interested the other person is in going deeper. In experiments by Kardas, Kumar and Epley, people who discussed meaningful questions with a stranger reported more connection and less awkwardness than predicted, and many who expected to prefer small talk ended up preferring the deeper conversation. Brooks uses this to argue that our reluctance to ask real questions is a forecasting error, not a sign the other person wants to stay shallow.
insights.when_to_use: When you notice yourself defaulting to weather and weekend plans with someone you would like to know better: a colleague you sit near, a new neighbor, a partner's friend at a party, a mentor.
insights.worked_example: At a conference dinner, a product manager is seated next to a stranger from another company. Instead of only trading job titles, she asks what has surprised him most about his field lately, and later what he would do if he were starting his career over. The conversation runs long, and they exchange contacts. Later she uses the same nudge with her brother-in-law, whom she has only ever discussed sports with, and learns he is quietly thinking about leaving his job.
common_mistakes: Jumping straight to intensely personal topics with no warm-up or consent; the research involved questions both parties answered.
Treating the finding as license to interrogate; reciprocity (you share too) matters.
Assuming everyone in every setting wants depth; read cues and offer an easy exit.

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Chapter 7 'The Right Questions' and Chapter 15 'Life Stories' (Epley's work referenced).
source.underlying_research: Kardas, M., Kumar, A., and Epley, N. (2022). Overly shallow? Miscalibrated expectations create a barrier to deeper conversation. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 122(3). Twelve experiments, more than 1,800 participants. Related: Epley and Schroeder (2014) on underestimating the pleasure of talking to strangers.

insights.confidence_rationale: Twelve experiments in a top journal with consistent effects, plus convergent findings from related work on talking to strangers. Caveat: mostly one lab group and mostly structured stranger pairings, so generalization to every workplace or cultural setting is less certain. Brooks's specific link to Epley here was confirmed via summaries mentioning Epley, not verbatim text.

insights.name: Ask big, open questions (crossroads questions)
insights.explanation: Brooks recommends questions that are open-ended and specific enough to answer, and that invite the other person to step back and look at their own life from a higher vantage point. Examples attributed to him in summaries include asking what crossroads someone is at, or what the next chapter of their life is about. He contrasts these with closed or dead-end questions, and suggests asking how someone came to believe something rather than just what they believe. Good questions make the other person the author of the conversation, not a witness answering a quiz.
insights.when_to_use: When a conversation is stuck at status updates; in mentoring, career conversations, reunions with old friends, long car rides with a partner, or first dates past the logistics stage.
insights.worked_example: In a quarterly career chat, instead of asking a senior engineer 'Are you happy here?', a manager asks 'What crossroads do you feel like you are at right now?' The engineer talks about wanting to try leading people but fearing losing hands-on work, which reshapes the development plan. On a weekend walk, the same manager asks an old college friend how she came to believe that moving back home was the right call, and hears a story about her mother's health she had never shared.
common_mistakes: Asking big questions cold, before any rapport or context, so they feel like a therapy intake.
Asking a closed version ('Are you happy?') that ends with yes or no.
Firing several big questions in a row without following up on the answer.
Not being willing to answer the same question yourself.
steps: Warm up with ordinary talk and accompaniment first.
Pick one open, specific question that invites reflection (crossroads, next chapter, how did you come to believe that).
Listen to the full answer, then ask a follow-up about the most alive detail.
Offer your own answer if it fits, keeping it brief so the focus stays on them.
Let it go if they deflect; offer the question again another time.
situations: Career conversation with a direct report
Catching up with an old friend

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Chapter 7 'The Right Questions'.
source.underlying_research: Indirect support from Kardas, Kumar and Epley (2022) on deeper conversation. Separately, Huang et al. (2017) on question-asking and liking is often cited in this area, but I could not confirm Brooks cites it.

insights.confidence_rationale: The general direction (open, deeper questions build connection) has research support, but the specific question wordings are Brooks's recommendations and have not been tested as such. Exact wording of his example questions was seen only in secondary summaries.

insights.name: Perspective getting beats perspective taking
insights.explanation: Trying to imagine yourself in someone else's shoes feels insightful but often does not make you more accurate about what they think or feel, and can make you more confident in a wrong guess. In a large set of experiments, Eyal, Steffel and Epley found that perspective taking did not reliably improve accuracy, while directly getting the other person's perspective (asking and listening) did. Brooks uses this to argue that knowing a person depends on asking and receiving, not on clever inference.
insights.when_to_use: Whenever you catch yourself thinking 'I know what they're thinking': predicting how a stakeholder will react, guessing why a partner is upset, assuming what a customer wants, planning a gift or surprise.
insights.worked_example: A director is sure her peer opposes a reorganization because he wants to protect his headcount. Before a tense meeting she asks him directly what worries him about the plan. His actual concern is that one client would lose its contact person mid-renewal, which is easy to solve. At home, rather than assuming his wife is annoyed about the in-law visit, a husband asks what part of the weekend she is dreading, and learns it is only the airport pickup.
common_mistakes: Treating empathic imagination as a substitute for asking.
Asking in a leading way that confirms your guess ('You're upset about the budget, right?').
Asking once and not checking back as circumstances change.
situations: Figuring out why a partner is upset

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023); summaries report he cites Nicholas Epley on perspective receiving.
source.underlying_research: Eyal, T., Steffel, M., and Epley, N. (2018). Perspective mistaking: Accurately understanding the mind of another requires getting perspective, not taking perspective. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 114(4). 25 experiments; one secondary source reports about 2,600 participants (not independently confirmed).

insights.confidence_rationale: Many experiments in a top journal, consistent pattern. Caveats: tasks were specific (reading emotions from faces, detecting lies, predicting a partner's preferences), the authors note perspective taking may help in conditions they did not test, and it does reduce egocentrism. The practical advice to ask rather than assume is robust.

insights.name: Looping: say it back and check
insights.explanation: Looping means paraphrasing what the other person said and asking whether you got it right, then letting them correct you until they confirm. It reduces miscommunication because speakers usually believe they were clearer than they were, and it proves to them that you were listening. Brooks presents it as a conversation-expert technique, and summaries report he cautions that doing it mechanically can feel unnatural, so a lighter paraphrase often works just as well.
insights.when_to_use: In disagreements, emotionally loaded conversations, when receiving feedback, clarifying requirements, and any moment where the cost of misunderstanding is high. Also useful in writing: restating a request at the top of a reply email before answering.
insights.worked_example: A client says the new dashboard is 'not usable'. Instead of defending it, the account lead says: 'So what I'm hearing is the data is fine, but your team can't find the weekly numbers quickly enough. Is that right?' The client corrects her: it is the filters, not navigation. In a different setting, a woman whose mother says 'You never call' loops back: 'It sounds like you feel I only reach out when I need something?' Her mother says no, she just misses hearing about the kids, which turns an argument into a plan for a weekly call.
common_mistakes: Parroting the exact words, which sounds robotic or patronizing.
Sneaking in your own interpretation or rebuttal inside the paraphrase.
Looping every sentence in a casual chat, which slows things down for no gain.
Skipping the check question, so you never learn you got it wrong.
steps: Listen to the full point before responding.
Restate the core of it in your own words, including any feeling you heard.
Ask a check question: did I get that right, or what did I miss?
Accept correction without defending your version and loop again.
Only once they confirm, give your response.
situations: Argument with a parent or partner

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), conversation chapters (Part 1); reported in reader notes and summaries.
source.underlying_research: Practitioner technique from mediation and conflict work (looping is associated with mediators such as Gary Friedman and Jack Himmelstein and was popularized by Amanda Ripley's High Conflict); I could not confirm whom Brooks credits. Related research on high-quality listening (for example Itzchakov and Kluger) is not confirmed as cited by Brooks.

insights.confidence_rationale: Widely used by trained mediators and consistent with research on reflective listening, but Brooks's treatment is short and the specific step format here is synthesized. Presence of looping in the book confirmed by multiple summaries; exact page and attribution not verified.

insights.name: Conversation as joint exploration (be a midwife, not a lecturer)
insights.explanation: A good conversation is not two people trading statements; it is shared exploration, where one person offers an idea and the other builds on it and hands it back. Brooks uses the image of a midwife: your role is to help the other person bring out their own thinking, not to deliver your conclusions for them. Practically this means building on what they said, asking how they arrived at a view, and resisting the urge to top their story with your own.
insights.when_to_use: Brainstorms, coaching conversations, dinner-table debates, helping a friend think through a decision, discussing politics or values with someone who disagrees.
insights.worked_example: A friend is torn about whether to take a job in another city. Instead of listing pros and cons from his own experience, the listener asks what parts of the new job she keeps thinking about, then builds on her answer: 'You said you light up talking about the team, what would you miss here?' She reaches her own decision. In a work planning session, a team lead uses the same approach with a junior colleague's half-formed idea, asking what problem it solves first instead of critiquing it.
common_mistakes: Topping: answering someone's story with a bigger one of your own.
Turning the exchange into a debate to win.
Steering toward the conclusion you already hold while pretending to explore.
situations: Helping a friend with a big decision

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Chapter 6 'Good Talks'.
source.underlying_research: No specific study identified; draws on conversation practitioners and the Socratic midwife metaphor.

insights.confidence_rationale: Coherent and widely shared advice, consistent with coaching practice, but presented by Brooks without empirical testing. Confirmed via a discussion guide and reviews quoting the chapter.

insights.name: Ask for the story, not the summary
insights.explanation: People make sense of who they are through the stories they tell about their lives, and they are usually eager to share those stories when sincerely invited. Drawing on Dan McAdams's work on narrative identity, Brooks suggests asking questions that invite narrative (how did you end up here, what was that period like, how has your view changed) and paying attention to how people frame their story, not only to the facts. The way someone narrates setbacks tells you a great deal about them.
insights.when_to_use: Getting to know a new teammate, interviewing, reconnecting with older relatives, deepening a friendship or romantic relationship, or writing a tribute or introduction for someone.
insights.worked_example: Before introducing a guest speaker, an events coordinator asks her not for her bio but how she ended up in climate finance. The story about a failed first startup becomes the heart of a much better introduction. At a holiday gathering, a grandson asks his grandmother what her first job was like and how she ended up in the city, and hears stories nobody in the family had recorded.
common_mistakes: Asking for facts (where, when, what title) instead of how and why.
Interrupting the story to relate it to yourself.
Judging how someone frames their story instead of being curious about why they frame it that way.
steps: Ask a 'how did you come to' or 'what was that like' question.
Let them take the time to tell it; resist redirecting.
Notice turning points and how they interpret them.
Ask about one turning point in more depth.
Reflect back what the story tells you about what they value.
situations: Getting to know a new teammate

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 3, Chapter 15 'Life Stories'.
source.underlying_research: Dan P. McAdams, narrative identity research (life story model). Summaries also note Epley's findings on underestimating the enjoyment of conversation.

insights.confidence_rationale: Narrative identity is a substantial research program, but its translation into conversational technique is Brooks's application rather than tested advice. Whether Brooks discusses McAdams's redemption versus contamination sequences specifically could not be verified.

insights.name: Serving a friend in despair: presence over fixing
insights.explanation: When someone is in deep suffering such as depression, the instinct is to advise, cheer up, or remind them of everything good in their life. Brooks, writing about his oldest friend Peter Marks, who died by suicide after years of severe depression, says those moves often backfire: advice signals you do not understand the illness, and what the person lacks is energy rather than ideas. What helps more is steady presence, acknowledging how bad it is without trying to argue them out of it, staying the same friend you have always been, and many small touches (texts, visits, notes). He also warns against assuming your own sad moments let you understand clinical depression.
insights.when_to_use: A friend, family member or colleague going through depression, grief, serious illness or a long crisis. Not a substitute for professional help when there is risk of self-harm.
insights.worked_example: A coworker returns from leave after her brother's death and is withdrawn. Rather than offering grief books or saying it will get better, her teammate sends a short message every few days ('thinking of you, no need to reply'), invites her to the usual Friday walk, and when she talks, says 'that sounds unbearable' instead of trying to reframe it. In a family case, a son whose father is depressed after retirement stops sending him lists of hobbies to try and instead comes over to watch the game every Sunday as they used to.
common_mistakes: Offering solutions or self-help tips to someone who lacks the energy to act on them.
Trying to cheer them up by pointing to their blessings, which can make them feel more alone.
Saying you understand because you have felt down too.
Disappearing because you do not know what to say.
Not taking risk signs seriously; presence complements professional care, it does not replace it.
steps: Show up and keep showing up; consistency matters more than eloquence.
Acknowledge the reality of their pain without minimizing or reframing it.
Hold back advice unless asked; ask what would help, if anything.
Keep being your ordinary self with them; normal company is a gift.
Send small, low-pressure touches that require no reply.
If you notice risk of self-harm, encourage professional help and contact crisis resources.
situations: Parent struggling after retirement or diagnosis

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 2, Chapter 10 (on serving a friend in despair), adapted from his NYT essay 'How Do You Serve a Friend in Despair?' (February 2023).
source.underlying_research: Primarily Brooks's own experience with Peter Marks. No specific study confirmed as cited. The advice is broadly consistent with mainstream mental health guidance for supporters, which is outside the book.

insights.confidence_rationale: The specific account rests on a single (deeply considered) personal case, so it is flagged. It is rated Medium rather than Low because the core advice (presence, validation, avoiding unsolicited advice and toxic positivity) aligns with widely accepted clinical and peer-support guidance. Timeline note: the essay says Marks died 'last April' and was published February 2023; one secondary source gave 2019, which looks wrong.

insights.name: Empathy as three trainable skills: mirror, mentalize, care
insights.explanation: Brooks breaks empathy into three parts: mirroring (picking up and accurately reading another person's emotions), mentalizing (working out why they feel that way, using your own experience as a rough guide), and caring (actually wanting good things for them and acting on it). He stresses that people differ in natural empathy but everyone improves with practice. Combined with the perspective-getting finding, the practical lesson is to notice the emotion, check your read by asking, and then show concern through action.
insights.when_to_use: When someone's reaction surprises you, when delivering bad news, managing a stressed team, or supporting a partner whose feelings you do not immediately understand.
insights.worked_example: A team lead notices a normally chatty designer has gone quiet in standups (mirroring). She guesses it might be the new review process making him feel micromanaged, but rather than assume, she asks privately how the change has landed (mentalizing, with checking). He says it is actually a sick parent. She offers flexible hours for the month (caring). The same three moves help a partner who notices her husband's irritability before a family wedding.
common_mistakes: Stopping at mirroring: feeling their distress without understanding or helping.
Mentalizing purely by projection and never checking the guess.
Caring in the way you would want rather than the way they need.
steps: Notice: name to yourself the emotion you are picking up.
Hypothesize why, but treat it as a guess.
Check by asking an open question.
Respond with a concrete act of care that fits what they said they need.
situations: Partner stressed before a family event

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 2, Chapter 11 'The Art of Empathy'; Chapter 12 'How Were You Shaped by Your Sufferings?' on hardship and empathy.
source.underlying_research: Draws on empathy research distinguishing emotional resonance, cognitive perspective and empathic concern (a standard split in psychology and neuroscience); specific studies Brooks cites could not be verified.

insights.confidence_rationale: The three-part breakdown mirrors mainstream academic models of empathy (affective, cognitive, compassionate concern), and trainability has some research support, but Brooks's specific studies were not verified. Summaries describe 'mentalizing by projecting one's own experience', which per the perspective-getting research should be checked, not trusted.

insights.name: Step back in hard conversations: talk about how you got here
insights.explanation: In conversations across deep differences (politics, race, class, family rifts), Brooks's chapter on hard conversations reviews the literature on difficult talk. One reviewer summarizes a key move: when a conversation becomes heated, break the momentum by stepping back together and asking how you arrived at this tense state, rather than pressing the argument. He also notes that people who feel unseen or marginalized bring that experience into what they focus on, so acknowledging their experience can matter more than debating the point.
insights.when_to_use: When a discussion with a relative, colleague or friend escalates; in cross-functional disputes; during political conversations at family gatherings; in tense performance discussions.
insights.worked_example: Two department heads are arguing in a meeting about budget cuts and voices are rising. One pauses and says: 'Can we step back for a second? I think we've each been defending our teams and stopped hearing each other. What do you need me to understand?' The temperature drops. At a holiday dinner, a daughter and her uncle hit the same wall over immigration; she says 'We keep going in circles. What experiences make this feel so important to you?' and the conversation becomes a story about his father's small business.
common_mistakes: Using 'let's step back' as a tactic to regain the upper hand.
Stepping back without then listening to what surfaces.
Expecting one conversation to resolve a deep disagreement.
steps: Notice the escalation signs: raised voices, repetition, interrupting.
Name the pattern without blame and propose a pause.
Ask how each of you got to this point or what is underneath the position.
Acknowledge the other person's experience, especially if they feel unseen.
Return to the topic only once both feel heard, or agree to continue later.

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 2, Chapter 9 'Hard Conversations'.
source.underlying_research: Reviewers say the chapter reviews the difficult-conversations literature; specific sources (for example Stone, Patton and Heen's Difficult Conversations) could not be verified as cited.

insights.confidence_rationale: The specific step-back move was confirmed in one review only, and the step sequence here is a synthesis. The approach is consistent with established conflict-resolution practice, but details of Brooks's chapter could not be read directly.

insights.name: Read the energy and the life chapter, not the type
insights.explanation: In Part 3, Brooks offers lenses for understanding someone more fully: personality traits (he favors the research-based Big Five, such as extraversion, conscientiousness, neuroticism, agreeableness and openness, over the popular but weakly validated Myers-Briggs), and the developmental tasks people face at different life stages (drawing on Erik Erikson and later developmental thinkers: establishing identity, building intimacy, consolidating a career, generativity, integrity). He treats these as prompts for paying attention, not boxes to put people in. Knowing what someone is wrestling with at their stage of life tells you what kind of conversation and support they need.
insights.when_to_use: Managing people at different career stages, mentoring, understanding why a parent or partner is changing, adapting communication style to a quiet versus outgoing colleague.
insights.worked_example: A manager has two reports: a 26-year-old eager to prove herself and a 58-year-old veteran who has become more interested in training others. Instead of offering both the same stretch project, she gives the younger one a high-visibility deliverable and asks the veteran to design onboarding. At home, a man realizes his recently retired father's new fixation on family history is about meaning and legacy, and starts asking him about it rather than teasing him.
common_mistakes: Typecasting people from a quiz result or a stage label.
Using Myers-Briggs as if it were a reliable predictor.
Assuming age determines life task; people reach these at different times.
situations: Managing reports at different career stages
Adapting to introverted or extraverted colleagues

source.citation: David Brooks, How to Know a Person (2023), Part 3, Chapter 13 on personality and Chapter 14 'Life Tasks'.
source.underlying_research: Big Five (Five-Factor) personality model, a strongly supported research framework; Erik Erikson's psychosocial stages (influential but less empirically precise). Other developmental sources Brooks may draw on (for example Robert Kegan) were not verified.

insights.confidence_rationale: The Big Five itself is high-confidence research; stage models are more contested and descriptive. Using either as a conversational lens is Brooks's application and is untested as a communication technique.

research_notes: Network policy blocked WebFetch for every non-allowlisted host I tried (zhurnaly.com, conorneill.com, www.mickmel.com all failed DNS resolution), so after three failures I stopped fetching and worked from WebSearch result syntheses only. Those syntheses drew on: Colgate news report of a Brooks talk; Joe Moran's review; Common Reader (Washington University) review; a church discussion guide PDF (squarespace) quoting Chapter 6 page references; SuperSummary chapter pages; Medium summaries; reviews by Bernie Gourley and others; commentary on Brooks's NYT essay 'How Do You Serve a Friend in Despair?' (Feb 2023); APA and Chicago Booth press releases on Kardas, Kumar and Epley (2021/2022); ScienceDaily and Greater Good coverage of Eyal, Steffel and Epley (2018); Penguin Random House and library catalog listings for metadata. I did not read the book text, the Penguin UK sample PDF, the NYT essays themselves, or the podcast interviews (Kate Bowler, RNZ, WHYY, The One You Feed) directly. Verified: Illuminators vs Diminishers; Chapter 4 'Accompaniment'; Chapter 6 'Good Talks' (attention as on/off switch, midwife image, joint exploration); Chapter 7 'The Right Questions' (crossroads-type questions); looping (mentioned in multiple summaries); Chapter 9 'Hard Conversations'; Chapter 10 on Peter Marks; Chapter 11 'The Art of Empathy' (mirroring, mentalizing, caring); Chapter 12 on suffering; Chapter 13 personality (Big Five over Myers-Briggs); Chapter 14 'Life Tasks'; Chapter 15 'Life Stories' (McAdams). The 'Essential Skills for Being Human' piece appears to be an NYT column (Oct 19, 2023), not an Atlantic essay; I found no Atlantic adaptation. Not verified: the exact wording of Brooks's sample questions, specific tips some summaries list ('favor familiarity', 'don't fear the pause', 'don't be a topper'), whom Brooks credits for looping, whether he cites Stone/Patton/Heen or Kegan or McAdams's redemption sequences, and the exact attribution of SLANT. The Eyal et al. participant count (about 2,600) comes from a single secondary source. Some search results were low-quality AI-generated pages (presentationbuilder.internationaltrucks.com and similar) and were ignored. Chapter numbering differs slightly across summaries; numbers given here follow the most consistent sources.
